snippet.title: Why Alexander made his soldiers shave #history #alexanderthegreat
snippet.description:
Before the Battle of the Granicus in 334 BC, Alexander ordered every man in his army to shave his beard. The reason had nothing to do with appearance — shaving denied the enemy a handhold in close-quarters combat. This is the level of detail that built the machine that conquered the known world.
The Macedonian phalangite was its foundation. A linothorax of glued linen layers. An open-faced Phrygian helmet. A shield sixty centimeters wide suspended from the neck by a leather strap — both hands occupied by the sarissa, an eighteen-foot cornel wood pike. The first five ranks projected their weapons simultaneously beyond the front line. Everything behind them angled their pikes at forty-five degrees to deflect incoming arrows. Total equipment weight: forty pounds — ten pounds lighter than the Greek hoplites they replaced.
Beside him stood the hypaspist — hand-picked elite linking the pike wall to the cavalry. Larger shield, shorter spear, pteruges protecting the thighs. His job was to guard everything the sarissa couldn't turn to face.
At the Granicus, Alexander crossed mid-afternoon against his generals' advice. When a Persian blade was seconds from splitting Alexander's skull, the hypaspist Cleitus the Black severed the attacker's arm at the shoulder.
The machine survived its first battle by one man's reach.

snippet.title: When Castles Were Besieged, Did Medieval Armies Attack Peasants Too ?
snippet.description:
When we think of a medieval siege, we picture knights and siege engines trying to bring a castle to its knees. But what about the people who weren’t directly involved in the fighting—the peasants living on the castle’s lands? Were they attacked too, or were they left alone? In this video, we’ll explore the fates of farmers, merchants, and day laborers to see what happened to them when their lord’s castle came under siege.

snippet.title: The Roman Merchant Who Tried to Follow the Silk — And Where He Stopped
snippet.description:
In the 1st century AD, Rome was losing an estimated 100 million sesterces every year to silk, spices, and eastern luxuries. The merchants carrying that gold east from Rome rarely made it past Antioch.
A Roman merchant joining a caravan east from Antioch was already at the edge of the Roman world. Beyond lay Parthian territory — deliberately hostile to direct east-west contact, their national wealth depending on transit taxes and controlled misinformation. The furthest a Roman merchant could realistically travel was to the Parthian border, where Sogdian traders took over.
The Sogdians were the professionals. Born into trade, fluent in six languages before adulthood, their caravans moving through territories Rome had never mapped. They carried the gold east through the Kushan Empire, across the Pamir Mountains, through markets where 36 languages were spoken simultaneously, across the Taklamakan Desert — a place locals called the City of the Dead — to Chang'an, a city of a million people that most Romans had never heard of.
Rome and Han China traded with each other for centuries. Neither empire ever made direct contact. The Romans called the Chinese the Seres — the silk people. They never learned their real name.

In the late summer of 52 BC, a Roman army under the statesman and general Gaius Julius Caesar surrounded the fortified town of Alesia. This marked the beginning of the last great battle of the Gallic Wars. The siege of Alesia was characterized by an elaborate blockade consisting of a double line of fortifications with massive walls, impassable trenches, and deadly traps built to isolate the town and starve the defenders. However, when a far superior Gallic relief army approached, it was unclear whether Caesar’s ramparts—and thus his legions—would prevail.
The siege of Alesia has shaped the modern perception of Roman siege warfare like no other. Many studies of siege warfare are based on a handful of famous events, with Alesia being the most popular example.INF  Caesar’s reliance on a blockade at Alesia often creates the impression that extensive earthwork was an integral part of Roman siege warfare and that the Romans relied primarily on blockades to conquer fortresses during the late Republic. However, the extent to which this was the case is questionable. To put Alesia into context, this video examines the 29 other reasonably well-documented sieges from Caesar’s  time. This will reveal how important blockades and earthworks really were for Roman siege warfare. But let’s start with the siege of Alesia.

snippet.title: Rome Never Crossed the Atlantic. So Why Is There a Roman Head in a Mexican Tomb?
snippet.description:
Rome ruled from Scotland to India, but largely ignored the Atlantic Ocean—the Romans called it Oceanus, the great outer sea. Medieval writers called it Mare Tenebrosum, the Sea of Darkness. Unpredictable winds, violent currents, no known destination. Their empire faced east.

But in 1933, archaeologist José García Payón discovered something impossible: a small Roman terracotta head inside a sealed tomb near Toluca, Mexico. The tomb dated to before European contact. The floors above it were intact—nobody planted it after burial. Modern dating placed the artifact between 184 BC and 616 AD. The discovery was buried in academic journals and forgotten.

In March 2026, the story resurfaced and went viral. How did a Roman artifact reach Mexico 1,300 years before Columbus?

Romans did reach the Canary Islands (the "Fortunate Islands" mentioned by Pliny and Strabo). The North Atlantic Drift—the same current system that carries Gulf Stream water toward Europe—could carry a disabled Roman merchant vessel from the Canaries to the Caribbean in 40 to 60 days. No crew needed. Just wind and current.

If even one Roman ship was blown off course in 800 years of maritime activity, the Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca Head stops being impossible. It becomes inevitable.

The artifact is housed at the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City.

• The French army built one of Europe’s first true artillery parks
• Cannons and field fortifications reshaped medieval battlefield tactics
• English commander John Talbot led a desperate assault against entrenched guns
• A single battle signaled the decline of the traditional knightly charge
• Castillon effectively ended the Hundred Years’ War and secured France’s victory

As thunder from dozens of cannons shattered the charge of English knights, the medieval world quietly gave way to a new era of gunpowder warfare.

snippet.description:
Play War Thunder now with my links, and get a massive, free bonus pack including vehicles, boosters and more on PC and consoles: https://playwt.link/sandrhomanhistory25 | Mobile: https://wtm.game/sandrhomanhistory25

In 1628, Europe was in flames. The plague had claimed thousands of lives, and the Thirty Years’ War had consumed many parts of the continent. Amid such epochal events, an inheritance dispute in the northern Italian Duchy of Mantua attracted, like a political vortex, the attention of the great powers of Europe and dragged them into a conflict they all wanted to avoid. This dispute quickly escalated into a thrilling war characterized by political intrigue and family entanglements. The War of the Mantuan Succession culminated in the siege of Mantua, a heavily fortified island city that was unintentionally quarantined by the blockade and thus spared from the plague—at least for a while. This is how contemporary historiography tells the story of the staggering siege of Mantua.

Outnumbered more than ten to one, they held the line through fire, famine, and weeks of relentless bombardment. When the final assault came, farmers, monks, and soldiers fought side by side and shattered the advance of an empire that had conquered Constantinople only three years before.

This cinematic historical documentary retells the impossible victory where faith, courage, and unity turned the tide of history.
On the walls of Belgrade, Europe’s fate hung by a thread until a miracle broke the siege, saved a continent, and echoed across the centuries.
